title: The second and third ways
hook: causes and contingent things point to a first cause and a necessary being

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first way: whatever changes is changed by another, and the chain rests on one moved by nothing. Your line was the unmoved mover. What did you watch move, and how far back did you follow it? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

At a family dinner, an old couple tells their story again. She nearly didn't go to the dance that night. Rain, a sore throat, a cousin who talked her into it at the last minute. Everyone laughs. Then a granddaughter goes quiet, because she's just done the math. If Grandma had stayed home, I wouldn't be here. A whole person, hanging on a cousin and the weather. Thomas Aquinas follows that quiet thought much further than one family. Not only, why am I here? But, why is there anything here at all? Today's word: the second and third ways.
screen: `SHE NEARLY STAYED HOME.` → `THEN I WOULDN'T BE HERE.` → `WHY IS THERE ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: The second way is a cousin of yesterday's. Yesterday was about change. Today is about being made at all. Thomas looks at the world and finds an order of causes, makers and what they make. A lamp shines because current reaches it. The current runs because something drives it. And nothing, he says, can be the cause of itself, because then it would have to exist before itself, which is impossible. Now, in an ordered line of causes, take away the first and you take away the rest. If there were no first cause, there'd be no middle ones, and no last one either. But there are causes, here, working. So there is a first cause, to which, Thomas says, everyone gives the name of God. The third way goes deeper, into the granddaughter's question. Thomas notices things that can be, and can also not be. Flowers. Mountains, slowly. People. They come to be and they pass away. They don't have to exist. Then he takes a bold step. If everything were like that, able not to be, then at some point there could have been nothing at all. And from nothing, nothing begins. So there would be nothing now. But there is something. So not everything can be the borrowing kind. Something must exist of itself, not lent its being by anything else, and giving being to the rest. This, Thomas says, all speak of as God. Readers have argued over that bold middle step, and tomorrow we'll come back to the arguing. Scripture says the giving part plainly. In Acts, in the Douay-Rheims, Paul says God is "he who giveth to all life, and breath, and all things." Every borrowed thing, on this view, is borrowing from someone.
screen: `NOTHING CAUSES ITSELF.` · `NO FIRST CAUSE, NO OTHERS.` · `THINGS THAT CAN NOT BE.` · `SOMETHING EXISTS OF ITSELF.` · then, large: `HE WHO GIVETH TO ALL LIFE, AND BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice something that didn't have to exist. Settle, and breathe. Look around and choose one thing. A mug. A sparrow. The person in the next room. Your own hand on your knee. Say to yourself, quietly: this didn't have to be. Let that sink in for a few breaths. It could so easily not have been, and here it is. Then choose a second thing, and a third. Don't hurry toward an answer. Stay with the surprise of it. If you pray, you can thank God that anything is here at all. If you don't, just let the question stand. The bell holds the time.
The second and third ways. Thomas's arguments from causes and from things that can fail to be: nothing makes itself, so there's a first cause, and something that exists of itself. Today's word.
screen: `THE SECOND AND THIRD WAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: why anything at all. Today, pick one ordinary moment, a meal or a face, and ask it once, without needing the answer. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

screen: `DAY 1157 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FOURTH AND FIFTH WAYS.`

howItsDone: Catholic philosophy courses often read the second and third ways together, the arguments from causes and from contingent things, and discuss where the third way's reasoning is contested.

notes: ST I.2.3 second way paraphrased: order of efficient causes; nothing its own efficient cause (prior to itself); no infinite series; 'to which everyone gives the name of God'. Third way: things possible to be and not to be; if all could not be, at one time nothing would have existed; from nothing, nothing begins; so something necessary of itself, causing necessity in others; 'this all men speak of as God'. Confirm.

The examples (lamp and current, flowers, mountains, the grandmother's story) are the script's illustrations; Thomas's text gives none in the second and third ways. The lamp is chosen as a cause working now (an ordered series), not a chain back through time.
'Readers have argued over that bold middle step' refers to the contested inference in the third way; no count or date given.
Douay-Rheims Acts 17:25: confirm exact wording ('he who giveth to all life, and breath, and all things').
